identity.name: Western Mexico shaft tomb tradition
alt_names: Shaft tomb cultures of West Mexico

correction.text: 'the western Mexican states of Jalisco, Nayarit, and, to a lesser extent, Colima to its south'; 'the valleys around Tequila, Jalisco' the 'undisputed core'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (no Cliopatria row), a culture area: central Jalisco as a 100 km radius around Guadalajara (Tequila lies 55 km west-northwest of it; 'Tequila' is not in the gazetteer) plus Nayarit and Colima. The region 'was not a unified cultural area' and 'At no time in the pre-Hispanic era did any political or cultural entity impose itself on the whole region' (footnote), so this is a culture, never a state.

region.text: Jalisco, Nayarit and Colima; the Tequila valleys the core

ledger.note: 300 BCE: the shaft tomb tradition develops in West Mexico. 'The shaft tomb tradition is thought to have developed around 300 BCE'; 'roughly dating to the period between 300 BCE and 400 CE'. El Opeño's earlier shaft tombs, 'dated to 1500 BCE', are 'linked to Central, rather than Western, Mexico'. The year is the page's round figure; the area is the researcher's reading of the three states.

400 CE: the shaft tomb tradition ends (end date disputed). 'The tradition lasted until at least 300 CE although there is not wide agreement on the end date'; the International Council of Museums gives 500 CE, the Smithsonian and Oxford 600 CE. The Teuchitlán tradition 'rises at roughly the same time as the shaft tomb tradition, 300 BCE, but lasts until 900 CE'; at Los Guachimontones the Tequila IV phase runs 'from 200 to 450/500 CE' and the Epiclassic 'from 450/500 to 900 CE'.

certainty.note: An archaeological culture area; soft everywhere.

sources.title: Western Mexico shaft tomb tradition

sources.note: Los Guachimontones phases (Tequila I–IV, Epiclassic 450/500–900), population 3,690–9,225, the segmentary-state vs chiefdom debate.

notes: Added at the orchestrator's request (the West Mexican shaft-tomb cultures). Type culture (post-3400 BCE; see the Olmec note). The Teuchitlán tradition (300 BCE–900 CE, Los Guachimontones; 'a segmentary state model' proposed by Weigand and Beekman in 1998 against 'lineage or clan-based chiefdoms') is the same core area continuing to 900; it is not given a dossier here (no page dates its extent or end beyond 'to 900 CE'), so the Tequila valleys 401–900 stay nobody's land unless a teuchitlan-tradition culture dossier is added. The Teuchitlán tradition page URL did not load. Wikidata id unknown. Gazetteer lacks 'Tequila' (Jalisco).
